newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end mostly higher, locals sell July.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end mostly higher, locals sell July.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended mostly higher amid rumors of export business to China and news a U.S. agricultural attache trimmed Brazilian soybean production estimates, pit sources said.

"There were a lot of unconfirmed rumors about China," said Roy Huckabay, vice president of LIT, a division of First Options. "My guess is that the rumors about China buying meal probably have some basis in fact but I can't confirm anything has been done."
Talk circulated early Wednesday that China was looking to buy U.S. or South American soymeal and soybeans.

Bullish fundamentals lifted old crop early and contract highs were notched in the May and July. The U.S. agricultural attache's cut in the estimate for Brazil's soybean output to 26.5 million tonnes was the catalyst, traders said.
USDA in April put Brazil's soybean output at 27 million tonnes. Attache reports often influence supply/demand data.
After the close, the U.S. agriculture attache in Argentina cut its estimate for Argentine soy production to 12.5 million tonnes from 13.25 million listed in USDA's April report.
Soybeans ended 6-1/2 cents per bushel to unchanged with July steady at $8.92.

New crop months ended higher amid expectations that new crop demand would grow as old crop prices rose. Some floor sources cited belief that Thursday's weekly USDA export sales figures would show an increase in new crop soybean sales.
Forecasts for below normal temperatures began to raise concerns. Some sources noted soybeans need heat units to develop, and a cold spring could slow crop development.

"I think we're starting to wake up to the fact that if old crop is tight and getting tighter, we need a big new crop yield," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Iowa. "Heat units are going to be watched."

The July contract was hit by techincal selling, led by local traders. Floor sources said one influential local trader sold one million bushels July near midday. The sale triggered sell-stops at $8.93 per bushel and prompted further local selling.

The new high for the July contract is $9.02 per bushel, topping the previous high of $8.99 set on Tuesday. It was the first time a July contract topped $9.00 since the 1988 drought. Contract highs were also set in May and August.

On the day, funds were aggressive sellers of at least 10 million bushels, keying off the market's inability to hold gains above $9.00 per bushel which chartists said was a bearish indicator. Goldenberg-Hehmeyer sold 3.5 million bushels August, Refco Inc sold 2.5 million July and Merrill Lynch sold one million July, traders said.

Unwinding of bull spreads was a major feature on the day, powered by ideas demand was growing for new crop supplies. Iowa Grain spread 800,000 bushels November/July at $1.84 to $1.82-1/2, premium July, LFG spread 1.3 million August/July at 32-1/2 to 33 cents, premium July, and Rand Financial spread 1.8 million August/July at 29 to 31 cents.
In options trade, Goldenberg-Hehmeyer bought 400 July $8.75 puts at 23 to 24 cents. Louis Dreyfus bought 400 August $8.75 calls and 400 August $9.75 calls at 21 cents.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 55,000 contracts, compared with Tuesday's actual volume of 58,340.
